Format Numbers the Same Way as SAS

Source: R/sas_round.R
sas_format.Rd

sas_format() formats numbers with a fixed number of decimal places so that the printed values match the SAS w.d format (e.g., 8.2).

sas_format(x, digits = 0, ...)

Arguments

x

A numeric vector.

digits

A single whole number between 0 and 15 for the number of decimal places to show. As in round(), and unlike format(), this is the number of decimal places and not the number of significant digits.

...

Formatting options, as in format(): width, justify, trim, big.mark, big.interval, small.mark, small.interval, decimal.mark, and scientific. Scientific notation is not used unless scientific = TRUE is passed, in which case the rounded values are formatted with format(digits = 15).

Value

A character vector the same length as x. As with format(), the values share a common width and names are kept.

Details

SAS formats do not round with the ROUND() function, so sas_format() does not use sas_round(). With the default DECIMALCONV=COMPATIBLE system option, SAS:

  • Rounds x * 10^digits half away from zero. Values within a relative 1e-16 of a halfway point (about one unit in the last place) are treated as halfway, so 2.675 (stored as slightly less than 2.675) is shown as 2.68 with two decimal places.

  • Shows at most 15 significant digits. When more digits are needed, the number is first rounded to 15 significant digits and zeros are shown after them (sas_format(123456789.123456, 10) is "123456789.1234560000").

  • Keeps the sign of negative numbers that round to zero, so -0.4 is shown as -0 and -0.001 as -0.00 with two decimal places.

  • Treats subnormal numbers (smaller than .Machine$double.xmin) as zero.

The tolerance is much smaller than the one used by ROUND(): 0.4999999999999982 is shown as 0, but sas_round(0.4999999999999982) is 1. So sas_format(x, digits) can differ from format(sas_round(x, digits), nsmall = digits).

These results were compared with about 100,000 results of the SAS 32.d formats (SAS Viya, V.04.00M0P060826), including every value with up to four decimal places in a range around zero. They are identical except within a few units in the last place of a halfway point, where SAS's tolerance varies from value to value, and when 15 or more digits are shown, where SAS's digits are not consistent (1/3 is shown as 0.333333333333330 with 15 decimal places).

With DECIMALCONV=STDIEEE, SAS formats the exact binary value instead (2.675 is shown as 2.67); sas_format() does not replicate that.

See also

sas_round()

Examples

format(round(1.005, 2), nsmall = 2)
#> [1] "1.00"
sas_format(1.005, digits = 2)
#> [1] "1.01"

sas_format(c(0.5, 1.5, 2.5, -2.5))
#> [1] " 1" " 2" " 3" "-3"
sas_format(-0.4)
#> [1] "-0"
sas_format(1234567.891, digits = 2, big.mark = ",")
#> [1] "1,234,567.89"
